491.title: Va'etchanan: the right and the good (Deuteronomy 6:18)
491.hook: do "that which is right and good"; the rabbis read it as going beyond the letter of the law
491.howItsDone: In Jewish ethics and law, acting lifnim mishurat hadin, beyond the letter of the law, is praised as the way of the pious, and some later authorities hold that a court may in certain cases press people to act this way.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the four places the Shema's words travel. Your line was at home and on the way. Where did you say something that mattered? Today, the last stop in this portion: a phrase that goes past the rules. Day four hundred ninety-one.

Two porters are carrying a barrel of wine for a rabbi named Rabbah bar bar Chanan, and they drop it. The barrel breaks. The wine runs into the dirt. By the rules of the time, workers who broke what they carried could be held liable, so the rabbi takes their cloaks as security. The porters go to a greater teacher, Rav, and complain. The story is in the Talmud, and it's built to make you squirm a little, because the rabbi with the broken barrel isn't exactly wrong. Today's phrase is what Rav tells him.
screen: `A BARREL OF WINE IN THE DIRT.` → `HE TAKES THEIR CLOAKS.` → `THEY GO TO RAV.`

segments.voice: Rav says: give them back their cloaks. Is that the law? the rabbi asks. Rav answers with a verse from Proverbs about walking in the way of good people. So he gives the cloaks back. Then the porters say: we're poor, we worked all day, we're hungry, and we have nothing. Rav says: pay them their wages. Is that the law? Yes, Rav says, and quotes the rest of the verse, about keeping the paths of the righteous. The Talmud has a name for this. Lifnim mishurat hadin. Literally, inside the line of the law. Not breaking the law. Standing back from the edge of it, where you could legally stand, and choosing to give more. Where does it come from? One root is today's verse from Va'etchanan: "And thou shalt do that which is right and good in the sight of the LORD." The medieval teacher Nachmanides, the Ramban, explains it like this. The Torah can't list every situation between neighbors and business partners and friends. So after all the specific rules, it adds a general one. Do the right and the good. Compromise. Give way. Go further than the line. The Talmud makes the same point darkly elsewhere: it says Jerusalem was destroyed because people judged strictly by the letter of the law and never went beyond it. A society can follow every rule and still be hard.
screen: `GIVE BACK THEIR CLOAKS.` · `PAY THEM THEIR WAGES.` · `INSIDE THE LINE OF THE LAW.` · `THE RIGHT AND THE GOOD.` · then, large: `BEYOND THE LETTER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: go beyond what's required once. Settle, and breathe. Think of a place where you're entirely within your rights. A refund you could insist on. A fee someone owes you. A rule at work that technically lets you say no. You're not wrong. Now picture Rav looking at the situation. Who's on the other side? What's their day been like? What would standing back from the line look like, just a little? Choose one place where you'll go further than you have to. The bell holds the time.
Lifnim mishurat hadin. Inside the line of the law. Choosing to do more than the rules require, because it's right and good.
Your line: beyond the letter. Today, in one place where you could insist on your rights, give a little more instead. Day four hundred ninety-one.

492.title: Eikev: not by bread only (Deuteronomy 8:3)
492.hook: "man doth not live by bread only", the lesson of the manna
492.howItsDone: Eikev is read in synagogues in late summer, and many Jews recall the manna each Sabbath, when two loaves are set on the table to recall the double portion that fell before the Sabbath.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the porters, the cloaks, and the right and the good. Your line was beyond the letter. Where did you give more than you had to? Today a new portion, Eikev, and a sentence people quote without knowing where it lives. Day four hundred ninety-two.

You've probably heard it. Man does not live by bread alone. It gets said about jobs that pay well and feel empty, about art, about weekends. Most people who say it think of it as an old proverb, or as a line from the Gospels, where Jesus quotes it in the wilderness. But it's a quotation there too. Its home is here, in Moses' farewell, and it isn't about bread in general. It's about one very specific food that fell from the sky every morning for forty years.
screen: `NOT BY BREAD ALONE.` → `A LINE PEOPLE QUOTE.` → `ITS HOME IS HERE.`

segments.voice: First the portion's name. Eikev means because, from its opening: because you listen to these laws, blessing will follow. But eikev is also the Hebrew word for heel, the same root as Jacob, who came out holding his brother's heel. Rashi plays on it: eikev points to the small commandments people tend to trample under their heels, the ones that seem minor. Then Moses turns back to the wilderness. In the old Jewish translation: "And He afflicted thee, and suffered thee to hunger, and fed thee with manna, which thou knewest not, neither did thy fathers know; that He might make thee know that man doth not live by bread only, but by every thing that proceedeth out of the mouth of the LORD doth man live." Hear the order. Hunger first, then a food no one recognized. Manna couldn't be stored; it spoiled overnight, except for the Sabbath portion. You couldn't stockpile it or own it. Every morning you depended again. And the point, Moses says, was a lesson: bread is real, people need it, but life doesn't come only from what you can grow or buy or keep. It comes from somewhere you don't control. He adds a detail to make it vivid: "Thy raiment waxed not old upon thee, neither did thy foot swell, these forty years." Forty years of walking, and their feet held. Not by bread only, Moses says. Not bread never, either. Bread, and more than bread.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: feed your spirit today. Settle, and breathe. Notice your body: hungry, full, somewhere between. That's the bread part, and it's real. Now ask the other question. What have you been living on lately besides food? News, scrolling, worry, work? And what actually nourishes you that you've let go thin? A walk, a text from an old friend, a page of something beautiful, a few minutes of quiet. Pick one, and plan when you'll eat it today. The bell holds the time.
Eikev. Because, and also heel. The name of the portion, from its opening word: because you listen.
Your line: not by bread alone. Today, feed something other than your stomach, on purpose, for ten minutes. Day four hundred ninety-two.

493.title: Eikev: not my hand alone (Deuteronomy 8:17–18)
493.hook: beware saying "my power and the might of my hand" earned this
493.howItsDone: Jews say birkat hamazon, the grace after meals, after eating bread, based on Deuteronomy 8:10, and many teachers pair it with the warning a few verses later against saying my power and the might of my hand.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the manna, and a line the world still quotes. Your line was not by bread alone. What did you feed besides your stomach? Today, what happens after the bread is plentiful. Day four hundred ninety-three.

Listen to almost any success story at a podcast microphone. I started in a garage. I worked eighteen-hour days. Nobody believed in me. It's often true. But the parents who covered rent, the teacher who noticed, the lucky timing, the country with roads and courts, the health that held: they usually get edited out. Not out of malice. Success just tells itself in the first person. Moses saw this coming for a people about to move from tents into houses. In the middle of Eikev he warns them about one sentence they'll be tempted to say.
screen: `I STARTED IN A GARAGE.` → `THE EDITED-OUT HELP.` → `ONE SENTENCE TO WATCH FOR.`

segments.voice: The chapter starts with gratitude. In the old Jewish translation: "And thou shalt eat and be satisfied, and bless the LORD thy God for the good land which He hath given thee." That verse is the root of the Jewish grace after meals, birkat hamazon. You eat, you're full, you bless. Then, right away, the warning. When you've eaten and are full, Moses says, and built fine houses, and your herds and silver and gold have multiplied, watch out that your heart doesn't lift itself up and forget. And the sentence: "and thou say in thy heart: 'My power and the might of my hand hath gotten me this wealth.'" In Hebrew, kochi v'otzem yadi. My strength, and the might of my hand. Then the answer: "But thou shalt remember the LORD thy God, for it is He that giveth thee power to get wealth." Notice what the verse doesn't say. It doesn't say you did nothing, or that work is pointless. Your hand was real. It says the power in the hand came from somewhere. Strength, health, wits, the land itself: given. The danger isn't wealth. It's the sentence, said in your heart, that erases everyone and everything that made the wealth possible. And notice the timing. Not in hunger. The warning comes when you're full. The same full stomach that leads to a blessing can lead to forgetting, and Moses puts the two side by side, a verse apart.
screen: `EAT, BE SATISFIED, AND BLESS.` · `WHEN THE HOUSES ARE BUILT.` · `KOCHI V'OTZEM YADI.` · `WHO GAVE THE POWER?` · then, large: `NOT MY HAND ALONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: credit someone for your success. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing you're proud of. A degree, a job, a home, a skill, a child who turned out well. Tell its story to yourself in one sentence, the way you'd tell it at a party. Now tell it again, slowly, and let the hidden helpers in. Who paid, taught, waited, covered for you, believed you? What luck did you get? Choose one of them to thank today. The bell holds the time.
Eikev. Because, and heel. The portion where Moses warns a full people about the sentence my hand did this.
Your line: not my hand alone. Today, when you tell a success story, put one helper back in it, out loud. Day four hundred ninety-three.

494.title: Eikev: what is asked (Deuteronomy 10:12)
494.hook: what does God require but to revere, walk in God's ways, love and serve
494.howItsDone: Following Rabbi Meir's reading of this verse, many observant Jews aim to say a hundred blessings each day, across the morning blessings, the prayer services and the blessings over food.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sentence to watch for when you're full: my power and the might of my hand. Your line was not my hand alone. Who did you put back in your story? Today, a question with a short answer. Day four hundred ninety-four.

By this point in his farewell, Moses has given his people a lot. The whole wilderness story, retold. The Ten Commandments again. The Shema. Warning after warning about forgetting. And the long run of laws, courts, kings, food, festivals, is still ahead. If you were standing in that crowd, you might feel the weight of it pressing down. How could anyone carry all of this? And right in the middle of Eikev, Moses stops, takes a breath, and asks the question for them, in the plainest words in the book. So what, exactly, is being asked of you?
screen: `SO MUCH SAID, MORE TO COME.` → `HOW COULD ANYONE CARRY THIS?` → `MOSES ASKS THE QUESTION.`

segments.voice: In the old Jewish translation: "And now, Israel, what doth the LORD thy God require of thee, but to fear the LORD thy God, to walk in all His ways, and to love Him, and to serve the LORD thy God with all thy heart and with all thy soul." Four things, and they fit in one breath. Revere. Walk in God's ways. Love. Serve. And the next verse adds a fifth: keep the commandments, for your good. Not for God's benefit. For yours. The rabbis couldn't leave the word what alone. The Talmud, in Berakhot, raises an eyebrow: Moses says what does God require, but to fear Him, as if fear of heaven were a small thing. Is it small? The answer given: for Moses, yes. Like someone asked for a large vessel who happens to own one; to him, it seems small. What's simple to state can still take a lifetime to own. And there's a playful reading too. The Hebrew for what is mah. Rabbi Meir, in the Talmud, reads it as me'ah, a hundred, and says a person should say a hundred blessings every day. So the simplest question in the book becomes a hundred small moments of noticing: waking, washing, eating, seeing something beautiful. A prophet centuries later, Micah, asks almost the same question and answers it with justice, mercy, and walking humbly. Two answers, one shape. What is asked is simple to say. The doing is daily.
screen: `WHAT DOTH THE LORD REQUIRE?` · `REVERE, WALK, LOVE, SERVE.` · `SMALL FOR MOSES, A LIFETIME FOR US.` · `MAH BECOMES ME'AH: A HUNDRED BLESSINGS.` · then, large: `WHAT IS ASKED IS SIMPLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one simple good thing. Settle, and breathe. Let the long list of things you're supposed to do today fall away for a minute. Ask Moses' question of your own day: what is actually being asked of me? Not everything. One thing. Maybe it's a call you owe, a kindness at home, a moment of real attention at work, a blessing said before you eat. Let it be simple. Then picture doing it, start to finish. The bell holds the time.
Eikev. Because, and heel. The portion where Moses boils a whole Torah down to one plain question.
Your line: what is asked is simple. Today, do the one simple good thing you named, and let that be enough for the hour. Day four hundred ninety-four.

495.title: Eikev: open the heart (Deuteronomy 10:16)
495.hook: "circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no more stiffnecked"
495.howItsDone: Jewish teachers often read this verse together with Deuteronomy 30:6 and the Talmud's teaching that the broken tablets were kept in the ark, as images of repentance, especially in the weeks leading up to the High Holy Days.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the plainest question in the book: what does God require? Your line was what is asked is simple. Did you do your one simple thing? Today, a startling picture of a closed heart. Day four hundred ninety-five.

Chapter ten opens with Moses remembering the worst day. The golden calf, the tablets thrown down and shattered at the foot of the mountain. Then God tells him: carve two new tablets like the first, and come back up. He does. And the rabbis add a detail the Torah only hints at. In the Talmud they teach that the broken pieces weren't thrown away. They were kept in the ark, beside the whole tablets, carried together through the wilderness. A few verses later, Moses tells the people what has to change in them so it doesn't happen again.
screen: `THE TABLETS SHATTERED.` → `CARVE TWO NEW ONES.` → `THE BROKEN PIECES KEPT.`

segments.voice: In the old Jewish translation: "Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no more stiffnecked." It's a jarring image, and it's meant to be. The Hebrew word is orlah, a covering, something that closes over and blocks. The Torah uses the same word for other blocked organs. Back in Exodus, Moses called himself a man of uncircumcised lips, his mouth closed, he felt, to speech. The prophet Jeremiah speaks of ears that are uncircumcised, that can't hear. So an uncircumcised heart is a heart with a layer over it. It knows things, but they don't get in. Then the second half: be no more stiffnecked. That's an image from the farm. An ox that stiffens its neck won't turn where the driver leads. And it's the exact word God used about the people at the golden calf: a stiffnecked people. So Moses is naming the old problem in two pictures. A covered heart doesn't let anything in. A stiff neck won't turn toward anything. Notice who's asked to do the opening. Here, it's the people: you circumcise your heart. Later in Deuteronomy, in chapter thirty, the same image comes back, and this time it's God who promises to do it for them. Commentators have held both for a long time: the opening is your work, and it's also a gift. The broken tablets in the ark make the same point. What cracked can be carried. A heart can be opened again.
screen: `ORLAH: A COVERING.` · `UNCIRCUMCISED LIPS, EARS, HEARTS.` · `A STIFF NECK WON'T TURN.` · `YOUR WORK, AND A GIFT.` · then, large: `OPEN THE HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: soften toward one person. Settle, and breathe. Let your shoulders drop, and notice your neck, the actual muscles. Is it stiff? Let it loosen a little. Now bring to mind one person you've closed over. Someone you've stopped listening to, or turned away from. You don't have to forgive anything. Just notice the layer. What is one true thing about them that you've stopped letting in? Hold it for a few breaths, and let your neck turn toward them, just slightly. The bell holds the time.
Eikev. Because, and heel. The portion where new tablets are carved, the broken ones kept, and a covered heart is told to open.
Your line: open the heart. Today, with the person you thought of, listen for one minute without preparing your answer. Day four hundred ninety-five.

496.title: Eikev: love the stranger (Deuteronomy 10:19)
496.hook: "Love ye therefore the stranger; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt"
496.howItsDone: Jewish communities cite the command to love the stranger in teaching about welcoming converts and newcomers, and many Jewish organizations ground their work with refugees and immigrants in these verses.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the covered heart and the stiff neck. Your line was open the heart. Who did you listen to without preparing your answer? Today, the last stop in Eikev, and the person at the edge of the room. Day four hundred ninety-six.

Remember your first week somewhere new. A new school, a new job, a new country. You didn't know where the bathroom was, or which jokes were safe, or whether anyone would sit with you at lunch. You watched everyone else move easily through rules you couldn't see. Most people forget that feeling within a year. They become the ones who know where everything is. The Torah, it seems, is worried about exactly that forgetting, because it comes back to this person, the stranger, again and again.
screen: `YOUR FIRST WEEK SOMEWHERE NEW.` → `RULES YOU COULDN'T SEE.` → `WE FORGET THE FEELING.`

segments.voice: Moses has just described God as great and mighty, the one who can't be bribed. And then, of all the things to say next: "He doth execute justice for the fatherless and widow, and loveth the stranger, in giving him food and raiment." The God of everything is described by who God feeds and clothes. And the next verse turns it into a command: "Love ye therefore the stranger; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." The Hebrew word is ger. In the Torah, a ger is someone living among a people not their own: a resident foreigner, without land, without family nearby, easy to cheat. Later, in rabbinic Hebrew, ger also came to mean a convert, someone who joins the Jewish people, and the rabbis read many of these verses about converts too. Both meanings are about someone arriving from outside. The reason given isn't an argument. It's a memory. You were strangers. In Exodus it's said even more sharply: "for ye know the heart of a stranger." You don't have to imagine it. You lived it, in Egypt, for generations. And the Torah won't let it go. The Talmud, in Bava Metzia, records that the Torah warns about the stranger thirty-six times, and some say forty-six. More than almost anything else. Not because it's complicated. Because it's so easy to forget once you're the one who knows where everything is.
screen: `GOD FEEDS AND CLOTHES THE STRANGER.` · `GER: THE ONE FROM OUTSIDE.` · `YE KNOW THE HEART OF A STRANGER.` · `THIRTY-SIX TIMES, SOME SAY FORTY-SIX.` · then, large: `LOVE THE STRANGER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: welcome one newcomer. Settle, and breathe. Go back to your own first week somewhere. Feel it again for a moment: the not knowing, the hoping someone would notice. Now look around your life as it is. Who's new? A neighbor, a coworker, a family at your kid's school, someone at your place of worship, someone who just arrived in your country. Picture one of them. What's one thing you know that they don't yet? Plan to offer it. The bell holds the time.
Eikev. Because, and heel. The portion that ends its teaching with the stranger, because you were strangers once.
Your line: love the stranger. Today, give one newcomer something you know: a name, a shortcut, a seat at the table. Day four hundred ninety-six.

497.title: Re'eh: see the choice (Deuteronomy 11:26)
497.hook: "Behold, I set before you this day a blessing and a curse"
497.howItsDone: Re'eh is read in synagogues in late summer, usually around the start of the month of Elul, when many Jews begin the reflection and self-examination that lead up to the High Holy Days.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ger, the stranger, loved because you were strangers once. Your line was love the stranger. Who did you welcome? Today a new portion opens with one word: look. Day four hundred ninety-seven.

Most of the choices that shape a life don't feel like choices while you're making them. You didn't decide to stop calling your brother. It just slowly happened. You didn't choose to scroll for two hours. You just didn't choose not to. Psychologists have names for it: defaults, habits, autopilot. Life comes at you as a stream, and the forks in the road go by without signs. The new portion opens by stopping that stream. Before it says a word about what to choose, it tells you to look.
screen: `CHOICES THAT DON'T FEEL LIKE CHOICES.` → `AUTOPILOT.` → `FIRST, LOOK.`

segments.voice: In the old Jewish translation: "Behold, I set before you this day a blessing and a curse." The first word, behold, is re'eh in Hebrew. See. It gives the portion its name. And there's a small oddity commentators love. Re'eh is singular: see, you, one person. But before you is plural: all of you. A whole people stands there, and each one is told to see for themselves. Nobody can look for you. Then the choice is laid out plainly. The blessing, if you listen to the commandments; the curse, if you turn aside. And Moses gives it a geography. When you cross the Jordan, set the blessing on Mount Gerizim and the curse on Mount Ebal, two real mountains facing each other near Shechem. Later, in the book of Joshua, the people do exactly that: half the tribes on one slope, half on the other, the blessings and curses read across the valley. A choice you can stand between and see with your eyes. And then two small words: this day. Not once, at Sinai, settled for good. Today, set before you again. Many Jewish teachers have read the whole of Deuteronomy as resting on this idea: that a person is free, and the road forks every day. The Torah doesn't pretend the choice is easy, or that it's always obvious. It asks for something earlier and simpler. See it. Notice that there's a fork at all.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one choice point today. Settle, and breathe. Walk through the rest of your day in your mind, hour by hour. Somewhere in it there's a fork you'd normally slide past without noticing. The first thing you pick up in the morning. What you say when you walk in the door. Whether you answer that message. Find one. Picture the two mountains facing each other there. You don't have to decide now. Just mark the spot, so you'll see it when you get there. The bell holds the time.
Re'eh. See, or behold. Said to one person, in front of everyone: the first word and the name of the portion.

Your line: see the choice. A week that went beyond the letter, lived by more than bread, credited other hands, asked simply, opened the heart, and loved the stranger. Today, when you reach your fork, stop for one breath and see it. Day four hundred ninety-seven.
